newsitem.title: UK: UK VAT receipts rise but fail to meet target-study.
newsitem.headline: UK VAT receipts rise but fail to meet target-study.

text.p: Value added tax (VAT) receipts collected in Britain rose by 3.0 percent in the last financial year but still fell short of departmental forecasts, a National Audit Office report said on Thursday.

Net VAT receipts rose to 43.1 billion pounds ($69.52 billion) in 1995/96 (April-March) but that was some five billion pounds below initial Inland Revenue/Customs forecasts made in December 1994 and 900 million below revised estimates set in November 1995.
A joint Treasury/Customs working group said the shortfall was due largely to better tax planning and tax avoidance by traders, and successful legal challenges to VAT law.
In November, the British High Court ruled that Customs & Excise acted illegally when it withheld payouts on claims for back-dated VAT extending beyond three years.
Although this case cost the tax collectors only a few million pounds other cases, including a major one on VAT payments on interest-free credit deals, could cost Customs much more.
The National Audit Office report noted that Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke plans to crack down on benefit fraud and tax evasion, in the hope of boosting tax revenues.

In last November's budget, Clarke announced measures to tackle benefit fraud that would cost 800 million pounds but claw back nearly seven billion pounds over three years -- the so-called "spend-to-save scheme."

The NAO said fraudulent tax and benefit practices came in many guises. "Current concerns include repayment frauds involving false identities, contrived liquidations, suppression of sales, false exports, excise smuggling and community transit fraud."
But a recent report by parliament's Treasury Select Committee doubted that the "spend-to-save" scheme could save anything like the amounts forecast.
"We are concerned that there is a risk that modest increases in expenditure on "spend to save" will not yield the forecast large increases in receipts over the planning period," it said.
The shortfall in VAT receipts is part of a continuing trend that has seen Britain's public sector debt consistently overshoot targets.

Britain's public sector debt in 1995/96 totalled more than 32 billion pounds, overshooting the government's target by some three billion pounds. But as high street spending picked up over the last few months and is expected to continue doing so, the tax take should rise accordingly in the current financial year.
In last November's budget, Clarke forecast a PSBR of 26.4 billion pounds for this financial year, falling to 19.2 billion pounds in 1997/98. City economists say those targets are attainable.
The National Audit Office report said the effects of the European single market, the black economy and the National Lottery also contributed to the tail-off in VAT receipts in 1995/96.
The first full year of receipts from Britain's National Lottery totalled 612 million stg, a rise of 508 million from 1994/95, the report said.
Overall, the Customs and Excise department collected 77 billion pounds net in taxes in the last financial year while the Inland Revenue netted nearly 97 billion pounds.
